name: Liver Brown
lede: Liver Brown is a dark, slightly reddish brown that comes straight out of the mineralogists' colour list, where it was defined as a recipe: chestnut brown darkened with a little black and olive green.

sections.title: A name from a mineral list
sections.body:
Liver Brown is number 106 in Werner's colour list, in the group of reds and browns, as Patrick Syme printed it in 1821 [1][4]. Werner defined it by a mixing recipe rather than a measurement: chestnut brown with a little black and olive green added [1]. The books I read give no account of why the organ was chosen, and the definition is all they offer [1][2].

Syme marked Werner's original colours with a W, but Baty finds slips, and liver brown is one that Werner had and Syme left unmarked [2].

sections.title: What Werner pointed at
sections.body:
Werner paired each colour with samples from the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms. For Liver Brown the animal samples are the middle parts of a hen pheasant's feathers and the wing coverts of a grosbeak, and the mineral sample is semi-opal [1].

Baty's plates make the same point with pictures: the cashew seedpod in Weinmann's 1737 botanical plates, an opal in Brauns's 1912 *The Mineral Kingdom*, and the wing feathers of the grosbeak in Gould's *Birds of Europe*, 1832 to 1837 [1].

sections.title: Its neighbours on the list
sections.body:
Liver Brown sits in a run of browns that Werner's followers copied with small changes [3]. Several late eighteenth-century lists in Baty, from Picardet in 1790 and from Widenmann and Kirwan in 1794, put [[reddish-brown]], clove brown, yellowish brown and tombac brown before it and [[blackish-brown]] after it [3].

The near neighbour is [[hair-brown]], defined as olive brown mixed with ash grey, so a greyer, greener brown than liver brown's reddish one [1]. One of the lists also places [[nut-brown]] just ahead of it [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
On screen the color is #513E32, which ISCC-NBS 1955 files as dark grayish yellow brown in block 46, 3.9 units away by ΔE [4]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards*, plate XIV, kept the name from his 1886 book, but its swatch is redder and lighter, near #65473E [4]. Werner's recipe belongs to a hand-painted list, and any modern swatch is an interpretation of it.

Our library files a Japanese traditional name, Mirucha, glossed as simmered seaweed, under the same swatch, which is a coincidence of color and not of history [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 6,676 carry a color within six ΔE units of this brown covering at least five per cent of the canvas, 28 per cent of the archive [5]. That is a common color: where it appears, 57 per cent of the matching colors sit in the shadows of the painting's lightness order, 41 per cent in the middles and 3 per cent in the lights [5].

By period it is steady from the 1200s, when 18 of 40 paintings in the peak decade carry it, down to the 1900s [5]. It is rare among Impressionists, with 19 of 140 paintings, and rarer still among Post-Impressionists, with 3 of 45 [5]. The painting with the most of it is Nagasawa Rosetsu's 1788 [[painting:cma-160688|Snails]], where it covers 98 per cent of the canvas [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match shows a screen color near this one and never proves a pigment [5].
